title: Holiness and Pentecostal Movements
summary: The story and teaching of the Holiness, Pentecostal and charismatic movements, from Wesley to Azusa Street to Nigeria's great churches, with a fair assessment of their strengths and dangers.
description: Holiness and Pentecostal Christianity has shaped the church in Nigeria more than almost any other movement. This course traces its roots in Wesleyan holiness teaching, the American Holiness movement and Keswick, the birth of Pentecostalism at Topeka and Azusa Street, the charismatic renewal, and the rise of Nigerian Pentecostal churches including the Aladura movement, Christ Apostolic Church, the Redeemed Christian Church of God and Deeper Life Bible Church. It closes with a balanced assessment.
objectives: Trace the roots of the Holiness movement in Wesleyan teaching
Describe the charismatic renewal and later waves
Trace the rise of Pentecostal and Holiness churches in Nigeria
Assess the strengths and dangers of these movements fairly
outcomes: Explain Christian perfection and entire sanctification
Explain the significance of Topeka (1901) and Azusa Street (1906)
Distinguish classical Pentecostal, charismatic and Third Wave
Describe the beginnings of CAC, RCCG and Deeper Life
Evaluate these movements by Scripture with charity

modules.title: The Holiness Movement
modules.intro: The Holiness movement grew from John Wesley's teaching on Christian perfection. This week we trace it through the nineteenth century.

lessons.title: Wesley and Christian perfection
lessons.body:
John Wesley taught that believers can, by grace, be made perfect in love in this life: loving God with all the heart and their neighbour as themselves (Matthew 22:37-39). He called this **Christian perfection** and taught it is received by faith, often as a distinct experience after conversion.

Wesley did not mean sinless perfection in knowledge or freedom from mistakes, but a heart cleansed from deliberate sin and filled with love (1 John 4:17-18).

He pointed to texts like "the very God of peace sanctify you wholly" (1 Thessalonians 5:23). Methodist preachers carried this message across Britain and America.

lessons.title: The American Holiness movement
lessons.body:
In the nineteenth century the **Holiness movement** grew in America. **Phoebe Palmer**, a Methodist laywoman, taught a 'shorter way' to entire sanctification: consecrate all on the altar and believe God's promise (Romans 12:1). Camp meetings drew large crowds.

Holiness churches were formed, such as the Church of the Nazarene and the Wesleyan Methodist Church. They stressed a second definite work of grace, separation from worldliness, and evangelism among the poor. The Salvation Army, founded by William and Catherine Booth (1865), shared much of this emphasis.

Holiness teachers began to speak of entire sanctification as a 'baptism of the Holy Ghost', language that prepared the way for Pentecostalism.

lessons.title: Keswick and the Higher Life
lessons.body:
In England the **Keswick Convention** began in 1875, teaching a 'higher life' of victory over known sin through full surrender and moment-by-moment faith in Christ. Unlike Wesleyans, Keswick teachers held that the sinful nature is counteracted, not removed.

Keswick strongly influenced missions. Hudson Taylor, Amy Carmichael and many others were shaped by it, and its emphasis on being "filled with the Spirit" (Ephesians 5:18) spread widely.

By 1900, many Christians across traditions were praying for a fresh outpouring of the Spirit and expecting God to restore New Testament power to the church.

modules.title: The Birth of Pentecostalism
modules.intro: In the early 1900s a movement emphasising the baptism in the Spirit with tongues began and spread worldwide. This week we study its beginnings.

lessons.title: Topeka, 1901
lessons.body:
**Charles Parham**, a Holiness preacher, ran a Bible school in Topeka, Kansas. Studying Acts, his students concluded that speaking in tongues was the evidence of the baptism in the Spirit.

On 1 January **1901** a student, **Agnes Ozman**, spoke in tongues after hands were laid on her; others followed. Parham taught that Spirit baptism, evidenced by tongues, was a third experience after conversion and sanctification, giving power for missions.

This 'initial evidence' teaching became a mark of classical Pentecostalism, based on Acts 2:4, 10:46 and 19:6.

lessons.title: Azusa Street, 1906
lessons.body:
**William J. Seymour**, an African American Holiness preacher who had listened to Parham's teaching, went to Los Angeles. In April **1906** revival broke out, and meetings moved to an old building on **Azusa Street**.

For about three years, meetings ran almost daily. People of many races and nations worshipped together, which was remarkable in segregated America. A newspaper, *The Apostolic Faith*, spread news worldwide, and visitors carried the message to Europe, Asia, Africa and Latin America.

As Joel prophesied, the Spirit was poured "upon all flesh" and "upon the servants and upon the handmaids" (Joel 2:28-29).

lessons.title: Pentecostal denominations
lessons.body:
New denominations formed. Some, like the **Church of God in Christ** and the **Church of God** (Cleveland), kept the Holiness three-stage pattern: conversion, sanctification, Spirit baptism. Others, like the **Assemblies of God** (1914), taught a two-stage pattern: conversion with progressive sanctification, then Spirit baptism.

A third group, **Oneness Pentecostals**, rejected the doctrine of the Trinity and baptized "in Jesus' name" only. Most Christians, including most Pentecostals, regard this as a serious error, since Scripture reveals Father, Son and Holy Spirit (Matthew 28:19).

Pentecostals stressed evangelism, missions, healing and the soon return of Christ.

modules.title: Pentecostalism in Nigeria
modules.intro: Nigeria has some of the largest Pentecostal and Holiness churches in the world. This week we trace their story.

lessons.title: Aladura and the 1930 revival
lessons.body:
In the early twentieth century, Nigerian believers formed prayer groups seeking God's power in healing and prayer. These **Aladura** ('praying people') churches included the Cherubim and Seraphim, founded through Moses Orimolade in 1925, and the Church of the Lord (Aladura).

In **1930**, **Joseph Ayo Babalola**, a former road worker, led a great revival at Ilesa with many reported healings and conversions, and people burned their idols and charms. This movement led to the **Christ Apostolic Church**, which became a major Nigerian Pentecostal church.

Some Aladura groups mixed Christian faith with traditional practices; others, like CAC, became more clearly Pentecostal and evangelical.

lessons.title: Missions and new churches
lessons.body:
The **Apostolic Church** from Britain worked with Nigerian believers in the 1930s. The **Assemblies of God** came to Nigeria in 1939, and the Foursquare Gospel Church followed later.

The **Redeemed Christian Church of God** (RCCG) was founded in **1952** by **Josiah Akindayomi**. From 1981, under **Enoch Adeboye**, it grew into one of the largest churches in the world, with parishes across Nigeria and many nations.

In the 1970s revival swept university and secondary school campuses through fellowships and the Scripture Union. Many of today's Pentecostal and evangelical leaders were converted or called in that season.

lessons.title: Deeper Life Bible Church
lessons.body:
In **1973** **William F. Kumuyi**, a mathematics lecturer at the University of Lagos, began a Bible study with a small group. It grew into **Deeper Life Bible Church**, formally established as a church in 1982, now with branches throughout Nigeria and many countries.

Deeper Life is a Holiness-Pentecostal church. It teaches salvation, entire sanctification as a second definite work of grace, and the baptism in the Holy Spirit with tongues; strict standards of holy living; careful Bible teaching through Bible studies and retreats; and divine healing.

Deeper Life is known for its emphasis on Bible study, simplicity of life, and evangelism, including large crusades and campus ministry.

modules.title: Renewal, Assessment and Lessons
modules.intro: This week we study the charismatic renewal and assess the strengths and dangers of these movements fairly.

lessons.title: Charismatic renewal and later waves
lessons.body:
From about 1960, Pentecostal experiences spread into older denominations. Episcopal priest Dennis Bennett's testimony in California drew attention, and renewal touched Anglican, Lutheran, Catholic and other churches. This became the **charismatic renewal**.

In the 1980s a 'Third Wave' among evangelicals embraced spiritual gifts without the classical teaching of tongues as initial evidence.

In Nigeria, many newer churches and ministries combine Pentecostal worship with charismatic teaching. Pentecostal and charismatic Christianity is now one of the largest forms of Christianity worldwide.

lessons.title: Strengths
lessons.body:
These movements have brought great blessings:

- **Zeal for evangelism and missions**: they have reached millions, often among the poor.
- **Expectation of God's power**: prayer, healing and deliverance, taking seriously the supernatural world that Africans know is real (Ephesians 6:12).
- **Holiness**: Holiness churches have called believers to separation from sin.
- **Lively worship and participation** of every member, including women and young people.
- **Prayer**: all-night vigils, prayer mountains and fasting.

Many Baptist, Anglican and other churches have been revived through contact with these emphases.

lessons.title: Dangers and a call to balance
lessons.body:
There are also dangers, which many Pentecostal leaders themselves warn against:

- **Prosperity teaching** that makes wealth a sign of faith (1 Timothy 6:5-10).
- **Experience over Scripture**: visions or prophecies accepted without testing (1 John 4:1; 1 Thessalonians 5:20-21).
- **Celebrity leaders** without accountability (1 Peter 5:3).
- **Fear-driven deliverance** that blames witchcraft for every problem.
- **Division and competition** among churches.

The answer is not to quench the Spirit, but to keep Word and Spirit together: "Quench not the Spirit. Despise not prophesyings. Prove all things; hold fast that which is good" (1 Thessalonians 5:19-21).

assignments.prompt: Write a history of one Nigerian Pentecostal or Holiness church (for example CAC, RCCG or Deeper Life): its founding, key leaders, teaching and growth. Then assess its strengths and any dangers it has faced, using Scripture.
